lead: Paul reaches one of the summits of his letter: the love of Christ urges us on; if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; God has reconciled us to himself and given us the ministry of reconciliation. “Be reconciled to God.” In the Gospel Jesus asks for words so true that oaths are not needed: let your “Yes” mean yes and your “No” mean no. A reconciled person becomes a truthful person. Psalm 103 sings: the Lord is kind and merciful.

set: Paul is still defending his ministry. Why does he work so hard, endure so much, and refuse to boast about outward things? Because the love of Christ has taken hold of him. These verses gather Paul’s whole gospel into a few lines: Christ’s death for all, a new creation, and reconciliation as God’s gift and the Church’s mission.
str: vv. 14–15: the love of Christ urges us on; one died for all, so that all may live for him.
vv. 16–17: we no longer regard anyone from a human point of view; in Christ, a new creation.
vv. 18–19: God reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.
vv. 20–21: we are ambassadors; be reconciled to God; he made him to be sin who knew no sin.
kw: The verb means to press, to hold together, to control. Christ’s love for us, shown on the cross, presses on Paul and directs his whole life.
From ordinary life: the making up of a broken relationship. Notice who acts: God reconciles us to himself. We do not win God back; he comes to us.
An ambassador speaks with the authority of the one who sent him. Through the apostles God himself is making his appeal.
vv: For the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all;
Christ died for all, without exception. The love that moved him is the love that now moves his apostle.
So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
Paul does not say only that the person is renewed but that “there is a new creation”. Baptism opens a new world. Isaiah had heard God say, “I am about to do a new thing” (Isaiah 43:19).
in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself,
The whole world is the horizon of God’s mercy. The cross is not God changing his mind about us, but God himself coming to make peace.
So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
Paul writes to Christians. Even the baptised need to hear again and again: be reconciled.
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Christ was sinless, but he took the place of sinners. Several Fathers, including St Augustine, read “sin” here as “a sacrifice for sin”, since the same Hebrew word can mean both sin and sin offering (in substance).
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in teaching that Christ, without sin, took our place: “For our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin” (CCC 602). It teaches that Christ entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to his apostles, and quotes Paul’s appeal, “be reconciled to God” (CCC 1442). Every Christian becomes a new creature in Baptism (CCC 1265). In the sacrament of Penance the priest still speaks as an ambassador of Christ: the words of absolution begin, “God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself.”

set: This is the fourth of the six contrasts in Matthew 5. The Law forbade false oaths and required vows made to the Lord to be kept (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21). In practice people sometimes swore by heaven, by earth or by Jerusalem, thinking that such oaths, which avoided God’s name, were less binding. Jesus answers that all of these belong to God, and goes further: a disciple’s plain word should be so reliable that no oath is needed.
str: v. 33: you have heard: do not swear falsely; keep your vows.
vv. 34–36: do not swear at all: not by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or your own head.
v. 37: let your word be “Yes, Yes” or “No, No”; anything more comes from the evil one.
kw: To call God or something sacred as witness to the truth of what one says. An oath assumes that ordinary words cannot be trusted.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:1: “Heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool.” Every so-called lesser oath still touches God.
Grammatically it can mean “evil” or “the evil one”. The need for oaths arises from a world where lying is common, the work of the father of lies (John 8:44).
vv: You shall not swear falsely, but carry out the vows you have made to the Lord.
Jesus does not deny the Law; he takes it to its goal. If no word is false, the oath becomes unnecessary.
But I say to you, Do not swear at all,
The aim is truthfulness in every word, not only in words spoken under oath.
And do not swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.
Even our own life is not in our control; it belongs to God.
Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’; anything more than this comes from the evil one.

St Paul uses the same language for his own honesty and for God’s faithfulness: in Christ “every one of God’s promises is a ‘Yes’” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The disciple’s truthfulness reflects the faithfulness of God.
ch: The Catechism explains that Jesus’ teaching on oaths belongs to the second commandment (CCC 2153). Following St Paul, who calls God as witness (2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20), the tradition of the Church has understood Jesus’ words as not excluding oaths made for grave and right reasons, for example in court (CCC 2154). An oath may be refused when it is demanded for purposes contrary to the dignity of persons or to the communion of the Church (CCC 2155). The heart of the teaching is simple: Christians are to be people whose word can be trusted.

qa: Is it wrong for a Christian to take an oath in court or at an ordination?

No. The Church teaches that an oath for a grave and just reason, such as in a court of law or when taking up an office, is permitted, because it honours God as the witness of truth (CCC 2154). What Jesus forbids is careless or false swearing, and a double standard where only sworn words are true.
study: Where do I need to be reconciled with God? When did I last receive the sacrament of Penance?
Do people know that my “Yes” means yes? Where do I exaggerate, shade the truth or make promises I do not keep?
